reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it discusses an Ulta retail promotion and a Carol's Daughter purchase, including a stated discount and total, in the context of an ordinary transaction. The receipt's $500 gift-card language is presented as a customer survey promotion requesting an opinion, not as a guaranteed return, and the product praise is identified as unpaid.

you have an ultra card that you get things from, so go ahead and sign up for that either online or in the store
This was a very good deal
I'm not being paid by them to say that
a $5 gift card to the first 100 people that come through their door

opening.argument: The video presents rewards as something viewers obtain by taking action. The speaker directs viewers toward an Ulta customer card, while the receipt shown in the video links an online survey action with a chance to win a $500 gift card. That combination turns an apparently ordinary purchase into a reward-acquisition pathway: shop, register, and complete an online step for a promised benefit. The presence of a purchase and a survey condition does not make the solicitation automatically trustworthy; it shows that the claimed reward is conditional on viewer participation.

citations.quote: you have an ultra card that you get things from, so go ahead and sign up for that either online or in the store

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this an ordinary promotion does not resolve the solicitation itself. The video pairs instructions to sign up with a prominently displayed $500 gift-card opportunity, yet does not establish who qualifies, how entries are verified, or whether the viewer will receive anything. The fact that the speaker bought a product confirms a transaction, not the reliability of the reward pathway.

citations.quote: go ahead and sign up for that either online or in the store

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited material shows a promotional survey drawing, not a guaranteed reward or deceptive acquisition scheme. The receipt does not promise that every participant receives $500; it describes a chance to win, and the spoken $5 offer is expressly limited to the first 100 people. The quotes therefore show conditions and ordinary retail participation, not an unsupported payout.

citations.quote: the first hundred people that come through they give you a 5 dollar gift card
a $5 gift card to the first 100 people that come through their door

opening.argument: Several reward signals appear together: an unusually large $500 gift-card headline on the receipt, a limited first-100-people offer, and multiple external links in the description. The speaker also uses personal experience and enthusiastic product praise to make the opportunity feel credible, saying the deal was very good and encouraging viewers to participate. Even if each element can be explained separately, their combination creates urgency, a high-value incentive, off-platform destinations, and testimonial-style reassurance. That is a meaningful pattern for a judge to treat as a reward solicitation rather than neutral information.

http://swagbucks.com/refer/mrsgiggels http://get.shopkick.com/snowdrop3022 http://ibotta.com/r/ek4dBA

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense isolates the $5 promotion and treats the $500 notice as harmless receipt language, but it does not account for the combined presentation. A large prize, scarcity language, several external referral URLs, and repeated encouragement to participate are exactly the features that can make a solicitation persuasive while leaving important conditions unclear. Unpaid praise does not eliminate those risk signals.

citations.quote: http://swagbucks.com/refer/mrsgiggels http://get.shopkick.com/snowdrop3022 http://ibotta.com/r/ek4dBA
go ahead and sign up for that either online or in the store

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The risk framing overstates what the evidence shows. The $500 item is a sweepstakes notice tied to sharing thoughts, not a promised return, and the spoken $5 offer is explicitly limited to the first 100 customers. The description's links do not establish that viewers must use them for the Ulta promotion, while the speaker expressly says she is not paid for the product praise. These facts weaken, rather than prove, a deceptive reward claim.

I'm not being paid by them to say that

opening.argument: Although presented as a personal update, the video functions as a direct promotional prompt. It names the retailer and product, highlights a discount, explains how to obtain the customer card, urges viewers to sign up, and closes with a positive assessment of the deal. The title itself advertises a free gift card, while the receipt supplies an additional high-value prize message. This framing steers viewers toward participation and purchase rather than merely documenting what happened to the speaker.

citations.quote: Free $5 gift card for Ulta beauty
go ahead and sign up for that either online or in the store
This was a very good deal

rebuttal.rebuttal: The speaker's disclaimer that she was not paid does not change the video's practical effect. Viewers are still told to sign up, shown the reward messaging, and encouraged to regard the transaction as a good deal. Calling it a personal update overlooks that the content supplies a clear participation prompt and advertises a free gift-card benefit.

citations.quote: I'm not being paid by them to say that
go ahead and sign up for that either online or in the store
Free $5 gift card for Ulta beauty

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A promotional tone is not by itself a scam. The content accurately describes a retail offer and a normal customer-card sign-up, while the speaker distinguishes her unpaid opinion from an official endorsement. The title's $5 wording and the spoken limitation to the first 100 people identify the actual offer; the receipt's separate survey drawing does not become a guaranteed benefit merely because it is shown.
